source: Hubert, Awa, Zabelina (2024) GPT-4 vs humans on divergent thinking, Scientific Reports
finding: On AUT, Consequences and DAT, GPT-4 beat 151 humans on semantic-distance originality at matched fluency.
numbers: Humans N=151, one model (GPT-4). Fluency matched by design: AUT human M=6.94 vs GPT-4 7.01 (p=.83). AUT originality group effect F(1,600)=622.10, eta2=.51; group x prompt eta2=.16. DAT semantic distance GPT-4 84.56 (SD 3.05) vs humans 76.95 (SD 6.13), t(300)=13.65.
limits: Human 'fork' score equalled GPT-4 'rope' (p=.989). Single model, 2023, two objects, semantic distance not human ratings.
agent_relevance: Open-mode metrics can be passed by a plain model. Semantic distance alone is not proof of useful novelty.

source: Hubert, Awa, Zabelina (2024) GPT-4 vs humans on divergent thinking, Scientific Reports
finding: GPT-4 answers were far longer, which inflates elaboration scores.
numbers: AUT elaboration GPT-4 M=15.45 (SD 6.74) vs humans 3.38 (SD 2.91), t(602)=28.57. Consequences elaboration 38.69 vs 5.45, t(621)=-36.04.
limits: Elaboration is word count, so it rewards verbosity.
agent_relevance: Length-normalise any open-mode score (matches guardrail G5).

source: Hubert, Awa, Zabelina (2024) GPT-4 vs humans on divergent thinking, Scientific Reports
finding: GPT-4 repeated a small word set on the DAT; humans were more idiosyncratic.
numbers: GPT-4 single-occurrence words n=152 vs human n=523 (69.92% share). Only 9.11% (n=97) overlap between groups. Top GPT-4 words included elephant (55) and symphony (51) among 151 responses.
limits: Descriptive counts; chi-square on unique vs single occurrence not significant (p=.211).
agent_relevance: High per-answer distance with low population spread: an early sign of mode collapse.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024/25) Divergent creativity in humans and large language models
finding: On the DAT, the best LLMs beat the average of 100,000 humans but not the most creative humans.
numbers: Human N=100,000. GPT-4 significantly above human mean; GeminiPro statistically equal to humans. Top human decile, quartile and above-median groups still scored higher than every model in the later list.
limits: Word lists only. Creative writing tasks (haiku, synopsis, flash fiction) used 3 models and DSI/Lempel-Ziv metrics, not human ratings.
agent_relevance: Models match the mean, not the tail. The agent needs a tail-seeking process, not one more sample.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024/25) Divergent creativity in humans and large language models
finding: Prompt strategy and temperature moved DAT scores a lot; opposition strategy hurt.
numbers: GPT-4 DAT rose with temperature (0.5, 1.0, 1.5); at highest mean 85.6, above 72% of humans (n=500 per condition). An etymology strategy beat the plain DAT prompt for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; opposition strategy lowered scores; thesaurus helped GPT-4 only.
limits: One task, mostly GPT-3.5/4. Weak models failed instructions more often.
agent_relevance: Hints that widen semantic reach (etymology, remote domains) are cheap operators; temperature alone is blunt.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024/25) Divergent creativity in humans and large language models
finding: GPT-4-turbo scored lower than GPT-4 and repeated words heavily; newer versions did not reliably improve.
numbers: GPT-4-turbo put the word ocean in over 90% of word sets. GPT-4: microscope in 70% of responses, elephant in 60%. Lower-scoring models were more variable and more often broke instructions.
limits: Word-frequency counts; model versions drift under the API.
agent_relevance: Pin model version and re-measure any open-mode benchmark.

source: Haase, Hanel, Pokutta (2025) Has the creativity of large language models peaked?
finding: Across 14 LLMs, AUT scores beat the average human but only 0.28% of responses reached the top 10% of human creativity.
numbers: 14 LLMs (GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude 3.5/3.7, Llama, Grok, Mistral, DeepSeek). AUT model means 65.66 to 77.85 percentile, all p<.001 vs 50. ANOVA F(13,356.64)=9.34. DAT: 495 runs below 50th percentile, 894 above.
limits: Percentiles against earlier human norms; no new human sample. Two prompt versions only.
agent_relevance: Average creativity is easy; the tail is not. Matches the Bellemare-Pepin ceiling.

source: Haase, Hanel, Pokutta (2025) Has the creativity of large language models peaked?
finding: A 2025 replication found lower DAT scores than 2023 GPT-4 studies: no gain in 18 to 24 months.
limits: Different model versions (GPT-4o vs GPT-4); may reflect alignment change. Direction (beats average human) held.
agent_relevance: Partial failure to replicate the level. Newer is not more divergent.

source: Haase, Hanel, Pokutta (2025) Has the creativity of large language models peaked?
finding: The same model and prompt ranged from below-average to exceptional on the DAT; naming the DAT in the prompt changed results.
numbers: 100 runs per condition per model. DAT-aware M=60.16 (SD 26.15) vs unaware 52.56 (SD 25.38), B=11.89, p<.001. Claude 3.5 d=1.82, Grok 2 d=1.08, o3-mini d=0.60; DeepSeek R1 Distill Qwen 7B d=-0.42 (worse). GPT-4.5: 6 of 100 runs below 50th percentile.
limits: Per-model effects differ in sign; alpha .005 used for interpretation.
agent_relevance: One sample is not a measurement. Sample many, select by code.

source: Haase, Hanel, Pokutta (2025) Has the creativity of large language models peaked?
finding: DAT is harder and less stable than AUT for LLMs; authors suggest a fixed-count distant-word list conflicts with local coherence.
numbers: AUT means tight (65.66 to 77.85 percentile) versus a wide DAT spread; authors cite Petrov et al. 2025 on underspecified tasks.
limits: Authors' interpretation, not a tested mechanism.
agent_relevance: The choice of metric changes model rankings; use more than one open-mode metric.

source: Stevenson et al. (2022) Putting GPT-3's creativity to the (alternative uses) test
finding: GPT-3 on the AUT: humans rated more original and surprising; GPT-3 rated more useful.
numbers: GPT-3 144 AUT runs (781 responses in tin can analysis) vs 42 humans. Humans higher originality (b=.17, p=.004), semantic distance (b=.10, p<.001), surprise (b=.14, p=.050); GPT-3 higher utility (p<.001). Originality-utility r=-.56 humans, r=-.61 GPT-3.
limits: Opposite direction to Hubert 2024 (GPT-4): different model generation, stimuli, scoring, human sample (reused data).
agent_relevance: Shows the originality-utility trade-off; the result flipped within about 18 months.

source: Stevenson et al. (2022) Putting GPT-3's creativity to the (alternative uses) test
finding: GPT-3 temperature did not predict flexibility; humans had higher mean flexibility but GPT-3 varied more.
numbers: Humans higher flexibility F(1,85)=5.53, p=.021. GPT-3 flexibility vs temperature r=.04, p=.80.
limits: Flexibility coded from category switches on one object (tin can).
agent_relevance: Category switching is not bought by temperature; it needs explicit category operators.

source: Wenger and Kenett (2025) We're different, we're the same: creative homogeneity across LLMs
finding: LLM creative answers are more like each other than human answers are like each other, on AUT, Forms of Fiction and DAT.
numbers: 22 LLMs vs humans (114 initial Prolific participants plus public data). Mean population variability LLM vs human: AUT 0.459 vs 0.738 (effect 2.2), FF 0.534 vs 0.835 (2.0), DAT 0.665 vs 0.819 (1.4); all significant.
limits: Embedding similarity; online human sample may itself include LLM use. Holds after controlling for response structure and same-family models.
agent_relevance: Ensembles of different models do not give independent creative samples (supports G4).

source: Wenger and Kenett (2025) We're different, we're the same: creative homogeneity across LLMs
finding: Creative system prompts raised individual originality a little but did not fix homogeneity.
numbers: Table 7: a more creative system prompt slightly raised LLM individual creativity (a less creative one lowered it); variability stayed far below human.
limits: AUT only, few system prompts.
agent_relevance: 'Be creative' instructions are weak; force structural diversity.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: Over 70+ LMs and a 26K open-ended query set, answers repeat within a model and across models.
numbers: 50 responses per query on 100 open-ended queries, 25 LMs detailed. Within-model: in 79% of cases average pairwise similarity exceeds 0.8. Across models mean pairwise similarity 71% to 82% (DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82, vs gpt-4o 0.81). 31,250 human annotations.
limits: Sentence-embedding similarity; temperature 1.0, top-p 0.9.
agent_relevance: Same-model and cross-model samples are not independent.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: Min-p decoding did not cure mode collapse.
numbers: With min-p, 81% of response pairs still exceed 0.7 similarity and 61.2% exceed 0.8.
limits: One decoding variant.
agent_relevance: Sampler tweaks alone are not enough; a structural change is needed.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: LM judges and reward models track human ratings poorly when answers are of similar quality but differ in taste.
numbers: Correlations between human ratings and LMs, 6 top reward models and 4 LM judges drop significantly on similar-quality subsets (25 annotations per item).
limits: Their annotation set; per-model figures in the paper tables.
agent_relevance: Model judges of originality are unreliable on close calls; use code and diversity checks (supports G5).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench
finding: On NoveltyBench (1,100 prompts, 20 models), frontier models gave fewer than 3 distinct answers in 10 samples.
numbers: 10 samples at temperature 1. Claude 3 and GPT-4o under 3 distinct on average. Cumulative utility of closed models below 4 of 10. Gemma 2 2B and Llama 3.2 1B showed the highest diversity.
limits: Distinctness by a trained classifier; some prompts rightly have one answer.
agent_relevance: Bigger is not more divergent. A usable open-mode metric: distinct classes in k samples.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench
finding: In-context regeneration (show earlier answers, ask for a different one) was the best prompt fix; paraphrase and system prompts barely helped.
numbers: 100 curated prompts, 8 generations, Claude 3 Opus, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Pro. In-context regeneration roughly matched human writer diversity; GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro exceeded human utility.
limits: Sequential calls and long context.
agent_relevance: Direct candidate operator: generate one at a time with earlier ideas in context; dedupe in code.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: 100+ NLP experts judged LLM-agent research ideas more novel than expert ideas, slightly less feasible.
numbers: Novelty means: human 4.84, AI 5.64 (p<0.05 with multiple-test correction), AI plus human rerank 5.81; 49 ideas per condition; 119 human vs 109 AI reviews.
limits: Ideas standardised in style; novelty judging is noisy (reviewer agreement 71.9% balanced accuracy); ideas not executed.
agent_relevance: Overgenerate and rank can produce reviewer-novel ideas, so selection matters.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: Overgeneration plateaus: of 4000 seed ideas per topic only about 200 were non-duplicates.
numbers: 4000 seeds per topic; duplicate = embedding cosine above 0.8; non-duplicate share in new batches kept falling and accumulated unique ideas plateaued.
limits: Threshold 0.8 set by manual inspection.
agent_relevance: Fluency has hard diminishing returns; budget must be dedupe-aware.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: The LLM ranker was only moderately accurate; authors say LLMs cannot yet evaluate ideas reliably.
numbers: Claude-3.5-Sonnet pairwise ranker accuracy 71.4% (Claude-3-Opus 63.5%) on ICLR-style review data.
limits: Proxy validation from public reviews.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model grade its own ideas without an external check (G5).

source: Zhang et al. (2025/26) Verbalized Sampling: how to mitigate mode collapse
finding: Verbalized Sampling (ask for several answers with probabilities) raised creative-writing diversity 1.6 to 2.1 times over direct prompting.
numbers: Poems, jokes, stories: diversity x1.6-2.1; human-rated score +25.7%; recovers 66.8% of base-model diversity. Larger models gain more.
limits: Authors attribute collapse to typicality bias in preference data; small models pay a quality cost.
agent_relevance: Cheap prompt-level operator for open mode; works better on stronger models.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) CreativityNeuro
finding: CreativityNeuro (weight steering, no behavioural data) raised DAT percentile and AUT originality and cut mode collapse.
numbers: Six open models (3B-14B). DAT percentile avg 94.1 vs activation steering 93.9; prompt-only activation steering 87.8; prompting 87.9. AUT originality avg d=+.36, surprise d=+.43; Task Task originality d=+.40, creativity d=+.24. Human raters N=720.
limits: AUT utility fell (novelty-utility trade-off). Needs weight access; small models only.
agent_relevance: Not usable on API models, but shows utility must be tracked alongside novelty.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) CreativityNeuro
finding: Baseline small models concentrate DAT words; steering spreads them.
numbers: Baselines put 25.5% of tokens on each model's top-10 words. 19 words recur in top-30 of three or more models (galaxy, quasar, xylophone in all three families). Steering cut top-10 share by 10.2 points and raised vocabulary entropy by 0.59 nats (+10%).
limits: DAT word level only; temperatures 0.9, 1.0, 1.2.
agent_relevance: Word-frequency entropy is a cheap code-side diversity metric for our agent.

source: Liang et al. (2023) Encouraging divergent thinking in LLMs through multi-agent debate
finding: Multi-agent debate targets 'Degeneration-of-Thought'; here 'divergent thinking' means argument diversity, not idea fluency.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive AR (200 items): GPT-3.5-Turbo 26.0%, +CoT 28.0, +Self-Consistency 29.5, +Self-Reflect 27.5, +MAD 37.0; GPT-4 51.0. About 0.63x extra inference cost.
limits: Does not use Guilford or Runco measures; judged on translation and arithmetic correctness.
agent_relevance: Terminology warning: debate raises accuracy on counter-intuitive tasks but is not a test of divergent production.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024/25) Divergent creativity in humans and large language models
finding: Cited secondhand: a brainstorm-then-select two-phase prompt raised GPT-3.5 AUT scores, in some cases past human levels (Summers-Stay et al. 2023).
numbers: Not opened; no figures taken.
limits: Secondhand citation, unverified.
agent_relevance: Fits a generate-wide then select-in-code loop; verify from source before relying on it.
